title: Password spraying against Windows accounts
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: A source address produces failed logons for many distinct accounts in a short time window.
investigation_steps: Pivot on the source address and time bucket; review targeted accounts, failure reasons, and whether any authentication succeeded afterward.
Compare the activity with the source address’s normal role, known VPN or proxy egress, and the affected accounts’ usual sign-in patterns.
If a success follows the failures, review the account’s subsequent sign-ins and endpoint activity in the same time window.
validation_notes: Confirm the failure event and account/IP field mappings in your identity logs. Tune the 15-minute window and account threshold to your normal authentication volume.
false_positive_notes: Shared NAT/VPN egress, identity-provider retries, password-manager errors, and authorized password audits can produce broad failure patterns.

kql.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4625
| summarize target_accounts=dcount(TargetAccount), failures=count() by IpAddress, bin(TimeGenerated, 15m)
| where target_accounts >= 10

spl.query:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4625
| bin _time span=15m
| stats dc(Account_Name) as target_accounts count as failures by IpAddress _time
| where target_accounts >= 10

sigma.query:
title: Password spraying against multiple accounts
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4625
  condition: selection
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security

title: Unusual PowerShell process execution
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: PowerShell launches with encoded, hidden, download, or policy-bypass arguments outside expected administrative activity.
investigation_steps: Review the complete process tree, initiating account, host, command line, and whether the parent process is expected for that user and device.
Pivot to child processes, file writes, script-block or AMSI telemetry, and network connections around the execution time.
Compare the executable path, signer, hash, and command pattern with approved administration and software-deployment activity.
validation_notes: Check process command-line and parent-process field availability. The query searches selected strings and will miss other forms of PowerShell abuse.
false_positive_notes: IT automation, software deployment, endpoint management, and incident-response scripts may use encoded or hidden PowerShell arguments.

kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("-enc", "-encodedcommand", "-windowstyle hidden", "downloadstring", "-executionpolicy bypass")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

spl.query:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 (Image="*\\powershell.exe" OR Image="*\\pwsh.exe")
| where match(lower(CommandLine), "-enc|encodedcommand|windowstyle hidden|downloadstring|executionpolicy bypass")
| table _time host User Image CommandLine ParentImage

elastic.query: process.name:(powershell.exe or pwsh.exe) and process.command_line:(*-enc* or *-encodedcommand* or *downloadstring* or *executionpolicy bypass*)

sigma.query:
title: Suspicious PowerShell command-line options
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - \\powershell.exe
      - \\pwsh.exe
  selection_args:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - -enc
      - -encodedcommand
      - downloadstring
  condition: selection_image and selection_args
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation

title: Potential LSASS memory access
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: A process other than an approved security or diagnostic tool requests access to LSASS memory.
investigation_steps: Identify the requesting process, signer, hash, command line, user, and parent process; confirm whether it belongs to an approved security or diagnostic tool.
Correlate nearby process creation, memory-access, file-write, and endpoint alert telemetry on the same host.
Review whether similar access occurs across hosts or is limited to a known maintenance window or software rollout.
validation_notes: Confirm your sensor records process-access events and that the query’s LSASS and source-process fields are mapped correctly. This is a lead for review, not proof of credential theft.
false_positive_notes: Endpoint protection, EDR, backup, diagnostics, and approved credential-management software may access LSASS-related processes.

kql.query:
DeviceEvents
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where AdditionalFields has "lsass.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, AccountName

spl.query:
index=sysmon EventCode=10 TargetImage="*\\lsass.exe"
| stats count values(SourceImage) as source_processes by host SourceUser
| sort -count

sigma.query:
title: Process access to LSASS
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 10
    TargetImage|endswith: \\lsass.exe
  condition: selection
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: sysmon

title: Unexpected scheduled task creation
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: A new scheduled task is created by an unusual account or with a command path outside approved software locations.
investigation_steps: Inspect the task name, XML action, trigger, principal, creator, and binary or script path.
Pivot from the creator and action to process, file, and network telemetry around task creation and first execution.
Compare the task and its execution cadence across similar hosts; check whether it aligns with a change or software deployment.
validation_notes: Enable and verify task-creation auditing; confirm task XML fields are available and correlate the creation event with process execution telemetry.
false_positive_notes: Software installers, endpoint-management agents, backup tools, and routine operating-system maintenance create scheduled tasks.

kql.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4698
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectAccount, TaskName, TaskContent

spl.query:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4698
| table _time host SubjectUserName TaskName TaskContent

sigma.query:
title: Scheduled task created
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4698
  condition: selection
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security

title: Registry Run key persistence
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: A process creates or modifies a common Run or RunOnce key to establish user or system logon persistence.
investigation_steps: Review the registry value data, user hive, initiating process, signer, file path, and whether the value points to an existing executable.
Pivot to file creation, process execution, and network events for the referenced binary, then check whether the same value appears on peer hosts.
Compare the change time and account with software installation, logon, or approved configuration-management activity.
validation_notes: Confirm registry event coverage and normalize key paths across 32-bit/64-bit views and user hives. Scope monitoring to autorun locations relevant to your environment.
false_positive_notes: Legitimate applications, installers, and endpoint-management software commonly maintain Run and RunOnce values.

kql.query:
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where RegistryKey has_any ("\\CurrentVersion\\Run", "\\CurrentVersion\\RunOnce")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName

spl.query:
index=sysmon (EventCode=12 OR EventCode=13 OR EventCode=14) TargetObject="*\\CurrentVersion\\Run*"
| table _time host User Image TargetObject Details

sigma.query:
title: Registry Run key modification
detection:
  selection:
    TargetObject|contains: \\CurrentVersion\\Run
  condition: selection
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: registry_event

title: Unusual Remote Desktop logons
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: Remote interactive logons originate from unusual source addresses or occur across multiple hosts in a short window.
investigation_steps: Pivot on account, source address, and time; review destination hosts, logon type, authentication package, and nearby failed logons.
Compare the source and account with approved remote-access gateways, administrator workflows, and the account’s normal host set.
Review activity after the logon on each destination, including process creation and additional remote logons.
validation_notes: Validate logon-type and source-IP mappings, and account for NAT, VPN, jump hosts, and event volume before tuning the host-count threshold.
false_positive_notes: Help-desk support, server administration, VDI, jump hosts, and approved remote-access tools can create broad RDP patterns.

kql.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4624 and LogonType == 10
| summarize hosts=dcount(Computer), logons=count() by IpAddress, TargetAccount, bin(TimeGenerated, 30m)
| where hosts > 2

spl.query:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=10
| bin _time span=30m
| stats dc(host) as hosts count as logons by IpAddress TargetUserName _time
| where hosts > 2

sigma.query:
title: Remote interactive logon
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4624
    LogonType: 10
  condition: selection
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security

title: WMI process execution
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: WMI provider processes launch command interpreters or scripting engines on endpoints where this behavior is uncommon.
investigation_steps: Review the WMI provider’s child process, command line, user, parent process, and host role.
Correlate WMI operational events and remote logons to identify the initiating account and any source host, then pivot to the destination process tree.
Compare the activity with software management, inventory, and monitoring tools used in the environment.
validation_notes: Confirm parent-process and WMI event coverage; provider process names can vary, and the query only covers selected child executables.
false_positive_notes: Configuration management, asset inventory, monitoring, and software deployment platforms often use WMI to launch processes.

kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wmiprvse.exe", "WmiPrvSE.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "rundll32.exe", "wscript.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

spl.query:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 ParentImage="*\\WmiPrvSE.exe"
| table _time host User Image CommandLine ParentCommandLine

elastic.query: process.parent.name:"WmiPrvSE.exe" and process.name:(cmd.exe or powershell.exe or rundll32.exe or wscript.exe)

sigma.query:
title: Suspicious process spawned by WMI provider
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith: \\WmiPrvSE.exe
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - \\cmd.exe
      - \\powershell.exe
      - \\rundll32.exe
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation

title: Valid account behavior anomaly
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: A valid account authenticates from unusual locations, at unusual times, or across an unexpectedly broad set of hosts.
investigation_steps: Compare the account’s source addresses, devices, locations, authentication methods, and target hosts with its established baseline.
Review MFA outcomes, conditional-access decisions, nearby failures, and any privileged actions after the sign-in.
Determine whether the account is human, service, or shared; compare the event with change windows and approved automation.
validation_notes: Build user- and service-account-aware baselines. Source IP and location can be distorted by proxies, VPNs, cloud egress, and identity-provider normalization.
false_positive_notes: Travel, VPN use, shared services, scheduled jobs, and changes in cloud egress may create legitimate location or host-count anomalies.

kql.query:
SecurityEvent
| where EventID == 4624
| summarize source_ips=dcount(IpAddress), hosts=dcount(Computer) by TargetAccount, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where source_ips > 3 or hosts > 10

spl.query:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4624
| bin _time span=1h
| stats dc(IpAddress) as source_ips dc(host) as hosts by TargetUserName _time
| where source_ips > 3 OR hosts > 10

sigma.query:
title: Successful logon for valid account
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 4624
  condition: selection
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: security

title: Phishing attachment execution
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: An email attachment is followed by execution of a script, archive utility, or newly written executable on the recipient endpoint.
investigation_steps: Correlate the recipient, message identifier, attachment name/hash, delivery time, and endpoint process start.
Review the full process tree and any files written or network connections made by the child process; pivot on hashes and affected recipients.
Check whether the same attachment or sender appears in other mailboxes and whether the execution pattern matches approved business software.
validation_notes: Join mail and endpoint events using stable message, recipient, file, or time identifiers. Email-client parentage alone is incomplete and does not establish that a file came from email.
false_positive_notes: Legitimate document workflows, add-ins, browser-based mail, and security tools can create similar parent-child or file-execution patterns.

kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe", "mshta.exe", "rundll32.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("outlook.exe", "winword.exe", "excel.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine

spl.query:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 (ParentImage="*\\OUTLOOK.EXE" OR ParentImage="*\\WINWORD.EXE" OR ParentImage="*\\EXCEL.EXE")
| table _time host User Image CommandLine ParentImage

elastic.query: process.parent.name:(outlook.exe or winword.exe or excel.exe) and process.name:(wscript.exe or cscript.exe or mshta.exe or rundll32.exe)

sigma.query:
title: Script host spawned by an email client
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - \\OUTLOOK.EXE
      - \\WINWORD.EXE
      - \\EXCEL.EXE
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - \\wscript.exe
      - \\cscript.exe
      - \\mshta.exe
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation

title: Suspicious Windows command shell activity
why: Deterministic analyst-authored hunt template. Validate table names and event fields against your telemetry before running.
hypothesis: A Windows command shell launches with discovery, download, encoded, or chained execution arguments.
investigation_steps: Review the full command line, parent process, user, device role, and neighboring commands in the same process tree.
Pivot on referenced files, child processes, destination addresses, and related discovery or authentication events.
Compare the activity with approved scripts, software deployment, troubleshooting, and administrative sessions.
validation_notes: String matching is a starting point, not behavioral proof. Confirm command-line collection and adjust terms for localization, quoting, and your telemetry schema.
false_positive_notes: System administration, installers, support scripts, and endpoint-management tools routinely use command shells and common discovery commands.

kql.query:
DeviceProcessEvents
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("whoami", "nltest", "net user", "certutil", "bitsadmin", "&&")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName

spl.query:
index=sysmon EventCode=1 Image="*\\cmd.exe"
| where match(lower(CommandLine), "whoami|nltest|net user|certutil|bitsadmin|&&")
| table _time host User CommandLine ParentImage

elastic.query: process.name:"cmd.exe" and process.command_line:(*whoami* or *nltest* or *certutil* or *bitsadmin*)

sigma.query:
title: Suspicious Windows command shell arguments
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith: \\cmd.exe
  selection_args:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - whoami
      - nltest
      - certutil
      - bitsadmin
  condition: selection_image and selection_args
logsource:
  product: windows
  category: process_creation
